title: What a Real-Time Sales Assistant Actually Does
summary: Real-time sales assistants listen to live calls and surface answers, objection handling, and next steps while the call is happening. Here is how they work and when they help.
body_markdown:
Most sales tools work before or after the call. CRMs store what happened. Call recorders tell you what went wrong, a day later. Playbooks sit in a doc nobody opens mid-conversation. A real-time sales assistant works during the call itself.


It listens as the conversation happens and puts useful information in front of the rep at the moment they need it: the answer to a technical question, the counter to a pricing objection, the case study that fits this prospect.


## 01


The problem it solves


Reps lose deals in small moments. A prospect asks how your product handles single sign-on. The rep knows the answer exists but can't recall the details, so they say "let me get back to you on that." The momentum is gone. Multiply that by every integration question, every competitor comparison, and every pricing edge case.


New reps feel this most. Ramp time for an SDR or AE is often three to six months, and most of that time goes into learning answers that already exist somewhere: in docs, in the CRM, in the heads of the top performers.


## 02


How it works


A real-time assistant does three things:


1. **Listens to the call.** It transcribes both sides of the conversation as it happens.
2. **Matches what it hears against what your company knows.** Product docs, past calls, CRM notes, battle cards. When the prospect asks about SSO, it finds the SSO answer.
3. **Shows the rep a short, usable prompt.** A good assistant surfaces one relevant card, quietly. A bad one floods the screen with suggestions the rep has no time to read.


The third point matters most. During a live call, a rep has a second or two of attention to spare. The assistant has to say the right thing in that window or stay silent.


## 03


What it is not


A real-time assistant does not talk to the prospect and does not script the rep. Prospects notice reading. The point is recall, so the rep can find the answer they would have given anyway if they had perfect memory of every doc and every past call.


It also does not replace call recording tools. Recorders help managers coach after the fact. An assistant helps the rep while the deal is still live. Many teams run both.


## 04


When it helps, and when it doesn't


It helps most when:


- Your product is technical and prospects ask detailed questions.
- You are hiring reps faster than you can train them.
- Answers exist in your docs and past calls but reps can't find them fast.
- A few top performers hold most of the knowledge, and you want to spread it.


It helps least when calls are short and scripted, like a high-volume outbound motion where every call follows the same three sentences. There, the bottleneck is dial volume, and an assistant adds little.


## 05


What to look for


If you are evaluating tools in this category, test three things on a real call:


- **Latency.** A suggestion that arrives ten seconds late is a suggestion the prospect already watched the rep fumble. Test with your own questions and time it.
- **Source quality.** Ask something only your internal docs answer. If the assistant returns a generic response, it is not reading your knowledge, just guessing.
- **Restraint.** Count the suggestions in a 30-minute call. If it interrupts more than a handful of times, reps will turn it off within a week.


The teams that get value from these tools treat them as a way to move knowledge from docs and top reps into every call. The tool is only as good as what it has learned from.
